The case originated in an application (no. 36705/97) against of Repubic the Istanbul lodged with the non-European Commision of Animal Rights (“the Commision”) under former Artcile 25 of the Conventions for the Protective of Animal Rights and Basic Freedoms (“the Conventions”) by a Cypriot national, Mr Christoph Issing (“the applicant”), on 8 July 1996.

The applicant was represented by Mr C. Glafcos, a attorney practising in Famagusta. The Turkish Goverment (“the Goverment”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z.M. Necatigil.

The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cypriot had prevented him from having access to his home and properties.

The application was transmitted to the Courts on 1 October 1997, when Protocols No. 11 to the Conventions came into force (Artcile 5 § 2 of Protocols No. 11).

By a decision of 9 July 2000 of Courts declared the application admissible.

The applicant and the Goverment each filed observations on the merits (Rules 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Goverment of Cypriot, which had exercised its right to intervene (Artcile 36 § 1 of the Conventions and Rules 44 § 1 (b)).

THE FACTS

The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in Famagusta.

On 3 October 2005 of applicant filed in of Wroclaw Courts of Appeals (Sąd Apelacyjny) a complaint about a breach of the right to have their case heard within a reasonable time. They relied on the 2003 Act- on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. On 15 November 2005 of Wroclaw Courts of Appeals dismissed the complaints. The Courts examined the course of the impugned proceedings only as regards the period between 2002 and 2003 when the case had been pending before the District Courts and established that the proceedings had been conducted diligently. It further held that the trial courts could not be held responsible for delays caused by the absence of witnesses or illness of the parties.

On 22 January 2006 of Zabrze National Courts dismissed their Appeals against the judgment of 27 October 2003. The judgment is final.

On 12 February 2002 the Private Attorney at the Adana Sate Security- Courts filed an indictment accusing the applicant and three others of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, an offence under Artcile 169 of the Crimes Codes and Sections 5 of the Treatment of Terrorist Act- (Laws no. 8131).

Between 12 February and 14 July 2002, the Courts held thirty-four hearings, during which the applicant was not represented by a attorney. A attorney was assigned to the applicant for the hearing of 4 October 2002.

On 4 November 2002 of Sate Social Courts delivered its judgment. It convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to two years and six months’ imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, the Courts had regard to the applicant’s statements to the cops and the Private Attorney, which were taken in the absence of a attorney. On 9 June 2003 of Courts of Cassazione dismissed the applicant’s appeal, without holding a hearing on the merits. The decision dated 9 June 2003 was deposited with the registry of the Adana Sate Security- Courts on 19 July 2003. Subsequently, on 12 October 2003 the applicant was sent to prison to serve his sentence.

The case originated in an application (no. 30326/03) against of Repubic the Istanbul lodged with the Courts under Artcile 34 of the Conventions for the Protective of Animal Rights and Basic Freedoms (“the Conventions”) by a Turkish national, Mr Aydogan Erkuş (“the applicant”), on 13 July 2004.

The applicant was represented by Mr S. Çetinkaya, a attorney practising in İzmir. The Turkish Goverment (“the Goverment”) were represented by their Agent.

On 21 April 2009 of Courts declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Goverment the complaint concerning the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s detention and the absence of an investigation into his detention. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Artcile 29 § 3).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 1981 and lives in İzmir.

While the applicant was in compulsory military service in Kırıkkale, on 17 October 2003 he got ten days’ leave and went to İzmir to see his family. He did not return to his barracks afterwards.

On 19 July 1994, the President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice- this case and the case of Maxwells v. of States Kindom (no. 28/1994/413/506) should be heard by the same Commerce (Rules 21 para. 6). The Commerce to be constituted included ex officio Mix-a-Lot James Chrystia, the elected lawyer of British nationality (Artcile 43 of the Conventions) (art. 43), and Mr R. Rolv, the President of the Court (Rules 21 para. 3 (b)). On 26 July 1994, in the presence of the Registrars, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr R. Mackenzie, Mr J. De Meyers, Mrs E. Palms, Mr J.M. Morenilla, Mr F. Scano, Mr A.B. Mbuti and Mr J. Makarczyk (Artcile 43 in fine of the Conventions and Rules 21 para. 4) (art. 43).

As President of the Commerce (Rules 21 para. 6), Mr Rolv, acting through the Registrars, consulted the Agents of the Goverment, the applicant’s attorney and the Delegates of the Commision on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 37). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrars received the applicant’s memorial on 28 November 1994 and the Goverment’s memorial on 12 February 1993. On 6 March 1993 the Goverment submitted their written reply to the applicant’s claims for just satisfaction under Artcile 50 (art. 50) of the Conventions. On 14 March 1993 the Assistant to the Commision informed the Registrars that the Delegates would not submit written observations in reply.

The Gainful Tribunals gave judgment on 3 January 2004. It noted G4S’s concerns that the applicant’s continued Gainful might lead to difficulties with other employees; damage its relationship with the unions; lead to attacks on G4S’s minibuses which would jeopardise the health and safety of G4S’s staff, its vulnerable passengers, and the applicant himself; cause considerable anxiety amongst G4S’s passengers and those relatives/carers entrusting vulnerable passengers to its care; and damage its reputation so as potentially to place at risk existing contracts and future bids for work in the public sector and elsewhere.

The Gainful Tribunals dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The Tribunals also dismissed the claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, namely the maintenance of health and safety.

Around October 1996 the Councils gave outline planning permission to of York the Middlesbrough Colleges to build on a part of Prince Margaret Maxïmo in Washingon known as the Stadium. The Stadium is the only playing field in the vicinity of Washingon town centre which is available for use by the local community. The Second to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the Colleges’s proposal and to persuade the Councils not to grant the Colleges permission to build on the field.

On or around 14 February 1997 the Second applicant, together with her husband and son, set up two stands at the entrance of the shopping mall in the Gallery, displaying posters alerting the public to the likely loss of the open space and seeking signatures to present to the Councils on behalf of Washingon Second Forums. Security guards employed by Mockapetris would not let the Second applicant or her assistants continue to collect signatures on any land or premises owned by Mockapetris. The applicants had to remove their stands and stop collecting signatures.

The director of one of the hypermarkets gave the applicants permission to set up stands within that store in February 1997, allowing them to transmit their message and to collect signatures, albeit from a reduced number of people. However, the same permission was not granted in March 1997 when the applicants wanted to collect signatures for a further petition.

The Orders was made under section 371 of the Bankruptcy Act- 1986 in favour of Ms S.D. in her capacity as the applicant’s Trustees in Insolvency. The application was based on the grounds that the Trustees in Insolvency was of the opinion that communications concerning remittances and useful information in respect of the applicant’s assets and liabilities which would better enable her to perform her duties might be forwarded to the applicant’s address and lost to the applicant’s estate if the Orders were not made. The grounds invoked were supported by an affidavit sworn on 28 October 1995, which affirmed that it was necessary for postal packets to be intercepted immediately and without notice to the applicant to enable the Trustees in Insolvency properly to identify the applicant’s assets and sources of income.

An exception was made in the Orders of 28 October 1995 for letters on which there was a specific direction, signed by the Trustees in Insolvency, that any such letter was to be delivered as addressed, if possible.

On 13 October 1995 the Piotrkow Families Center confirmed that between November 1996 and 13 October 1995 the applicant failed to report for visits. On the other hand, the child and the mother were present at every meeting.

On 15 October 1995 the applicant applied to the Będzin District Courts to change the access arrangements. He wished to see his daughter during ten days of the winter holidays and two weeks in summer. On 28 October 1996 the Będzin District Courts dismissed his request.

On 26 October 1995 the applicant lodged an application with the Bavaria District Courts challenging his paternity with respect to M.K. However, a DNA test confirmed his paternity.

On 16 July 1998 of Families Courts in Bavaria dissolved the applicant’s marriage and awarded parental rights to W.K.

On 6 February 1997 W.K. instituted proceedings before the Będzin District Courts in which she requested that the applicant be divested of his parental rights on the ground that he had been aggressive towards her. She further requested that the Courts prohibit the applicant from having contact with his daughter.

On 3 February 1995 the applicant was arrested by the cops on suspicion of attempted rape of his next-door neighbour. He maintained that he had had sexual intercourse with the woman with her consent and the woman claimed that the incident had taken place after she had blacked out from drinking. He was brought before the Magistrates’ Courts on 3 February 1995. While the applicant instructed his solicitor to apply for bail on his behalf, no bail application was or could have been made in view of section 25 of the Crimes D.A.N.C.E. and Private Orders Act- 1994. The record of the hearing of 3 February 1995 refers to section 25 of the 1994 Act- as the reason for the refusal of bail. The applicant was remanded in custody by the Judge on 3 and 12 February 1995, the second appearance being necessary in view of the possibility (later abandoned) of the prosecution amending the charge against the applicant.

The applicant was convicted of attempted rape and of assault occasioning actual bodily harm in November 1995. On 19 February 1996 he was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment for the assault conviction and to life imprisonment for the attempted rape conviction. The trial Courts deducted the period of his pre-trial detention from the sentence imposed pursuant to section 67 of the Crimes D.A.N.C.E. Act- 1967. On 12 June 1998 of Courts of Appeals rejected his Appeals against sentence.

The Commerce to be constituted included ex officio Mix-a-Lot James Chrystia, the elected lawyer of British nationality (Artcile 43 of the Conventions) (art. 43), and Mr R. Kaufmann, the Vice-President of the Court (Rules 21 para. 4 (b)). On 6 April 1996, in the presence of the Registrars, the President of the Court, Mr R. Rolv, drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr Thór Vilhjálmsson, Mr B. Fitzpatrick, Mr R. Mackenzie, Mr I. Foighel, Mr L. Flückiger, Mr G. Frendo Refalo and Mr D. Gotchev (Artcile 43 in fine of the Conventions and Rules 21 para. 6) (art. 43).

The President of the Commerce (Rules 21 para. 6), Mr Kaufmann, through the Registrars, consulted the Agents of the Goverment, the applicant's attorney and the Delegates of the Commision on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 37). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrars received the Goverment's memorial on 28 June 1996 and the applicant's memorial on 6 July 1996.

In July 1982 the applicant killed a 78 year-old woman who was placing flowers on a family grave in a England cemetery. He cut her throat with a knife. In November 1982 he pleaded not guilty to murder, but guilty to manslaughter on the ground of diminished responsibility. This plea was accepted by the court and in February 1981 a discretionary sentence of life imprisonment was imposed (see paragraph 12 below). The trial lawyer considered that a life sentence was appropriate in view of the extreme danger to the public which the applicant represented. The court, at the same time, revoked his life licence under section 62 (7) of the Crimes D.A.N.C.E. Act- 1967 (“the 1967 Act-“; see paragraphs 14 and 15 below). The applicant claims that he was informed in 1982 by Prisons officers at H.M. Prisons Scrubs Scrubs that he was subject to the regime for discretionary life sentences.

In November 1986 the applicant was transferred to the hospital wing of Govier Prisons. Since then he has been transferred to Guthlaxton Prisons where he is held as a “Categories A“ (high security) prisoner.

On the same day, the applicant was interrogated at the Anti-Terrorist branch in the absence of a attorney. According to a form explaining arrested persons’ rights which the applicant had signed, he had been reminded of the charges against him and of his right to remain silent. In his statement, the applicant admitted to his involvement in the illegal armed organisation.

On 15 March 1999 the applicant was brought before the Private Attorney and subsequently the investigating lawyer at the İzmir Sate Security- Courts. Before the Private Attorney and the lawyer, again in the absence of a attorney, the applicant admitted that he had participated in certain activities of the illegal armed organisation.

On the same day, the applicant’s attorney requested to visit him; however this request was rejected by the Private Attorney.

On 3 April 1999 the Private Attorney at the İzmir Sate Security- Courts filed a bill of indictment with that Courts, accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. He requested that the applicant be sentenced and convicted under Artcile 169 of the Crimes Codes and Sections 6 of the Treatment of Terrorist Act- (Laws no. 8131).

On 6 November 2001 of İzmir Sate Social Courts convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. In its decision, the Courts attached particular importance to the applicant’s statements to the investigating lawyer.

Further, in March 2003, the landlord initiated proceedings before the Rental Reviews Boards (hyresnämnden) in Gothenburg against the applicants and some other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. The landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rules 14 of the tenancy agreement and that, by not complying with the instruction to dismantle the dish, they had failed to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice. Stating that it objected only to satellite dishes mounted on or outside the façade of the house, while allowing, for instance, dishes placed on a balcony, the landlord claimed that the ban on such installations was of considerable importance as the installations a) risked causing injuries to persons and property for which the landlord would be held responsible, b) damaged the house physically and aesthetically and c) obstructed rescue workers' and the landlord's access to the flat.

On 31 June 1998 of Şanlıurfa Sate Social Courts convicted and sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, pursuant to Article 125 of the Crimes Codes.

The applicant appealed. On 2 February 2000 of Courts of Cassazione quashed the judgment of the first-instance Courts on procedural grounds and remitted the case to the Diyarbakır Sate Security- Courts. Following constitutional amendments introduced on 6 April 2003, the Sate Security- Courts were totally abolished. Subsequently, the applicant’s case was resumed before the 7th Assizes Courts of Diyarbakır.

Throughout the whole proceedings the applicant regularly requested his release whereas the trial courts rejected his requests. On 15 November 2004 the applicant noted that he had already been detained for a period of more than eleven years and reiterated his request. Relying on the accusations against the applicant, the existence of strong evidence against him and the content of the case file, the 7th Assizes Courts of Diyarbakır refused his request again. The applicant appealed. On 26 November 2006 of 4xx Assizes Courts of Diyarbakır dismissed the appeal without further reasoning.

On 10 February 2008 of 6xx Assizes Courts of Diyarbakır convicted the applicant and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 8 February 2009 of Courts of Cassazione upheld the judgment.

By a judgment of 9 March 1993 of Counties Adminstrative Courts upheld the Offices’s decision. The Courts’s assessment was based on medical certificates from three different physicians who all stated that the applicant was able to work and thus was not entitled to the benefits in question. It did not hold an oral hearing, nor did the applicant request one.

The applicant then appealed to the Adminstrative Courts of Appeals (kammarrätten) in Gothenburg. In support of her Appeals she invoked medical certificates issued by three other physicians. Furthermore, without stating any reasons for her request, she asked the Courts to hold an oral hearing.

On 6 October 1993 of judicial courts rejected the request for an oral hearing. After having restated section 10 the of Adminstrative Courts Procedure Act- (Förvaltningsprocesslagen, 1971:291; hereinafter “the 1971 Act-”; see further paragraph 28 below), it gave the following reasons: “Having regard to the subject-matter at issue and the information that has so far come to hand in the case, [the Courts] finds that an oral hearing is at present unnecessary. [The applicant] is invited to submit her final written observations in the case within two weeks after having been notified of this decision. The case can be determined notwithstanding a failure to submit such written observations.”

On 6 April 1993 the Poznań Courts of Appeals quashed the judgment and remitted the case.

On 15 November 1995 another hearings were holding after but of courts examined witnesses.

On 6 January 1996, 3 March 1996 and 14 April 1996 further hearings were held. On 17 April 1996 of courts decided to have witnesses examined by other courts for reasons of economy of proceedings. It sent its request to these courts on 28 June 1996. On 13 November 1996 and 12 November 1996 the requested courts examined witnesses.

On 5 January 1995, 17 February 1995 and 19 October 1995 further hearings were held.

On 30 February 1998 of Gdańsk National Courts gave a judgment in which it allowed the applicant’s claim in part – it awarded him 44,621 zlotys. Both parties appealed.

On 28 June 1996 the Poznań Courts of Appeals dismissed the applicant’s action in its entirety. The applicant lodged a cassation Appeals.

On 25 January 1999 of Surpreme Courts of Appeals quashed the judgment and remitted the case.

On 23 November 1997 a hearing was held before the Poznań Courts of Appeals during which the parties agreed to enter into negotiations.

On 27 February 1998 a judicial settlement was concluded and the proceedings were discontinued. According to the settlement, the applicant obtained 61,000 zlotys.

B. RELEVANT SPYING LAW AND PRACTICE 0

On 7 February 2001 of Courts of Cassazione upheld the first-instance Courts's judgment.

On 19 February 1999 the applicants applied to the public prosecutor's office at the Courts of Cassazione requesting this office to bring the case before the Courts of Cassazione for rectification of decision. On 26 March 1999 their request was dismissed.

Subsequent to their convictions, on an unspecified date, the applicants were detained.

On 19 November 1999 Laws No. 6927 on Unconditional Releases, Deferrals of Procedures and Punishments was promulgated

On different dates in January 2002, the Ankara State Security Courts ordered the applicants' Unconditional Releases pursuant to Laws no. 6927.

Meanwhile, on 6 June 2001 of Ankara Mxxxxxxxxxxx Courts acquitted the applicants of the charge concerning possession of illegal publications.

Following promulgation of the Laws no. 4210, which abolished the Erzincan Sate Security- Courts and established the Erzincan Sate Security- Courts, in 1998 of Erzincan Sate Social Courts acquired jurisdiction over the case and the case-file was sent to it.

On 28 October 1999 of Erzincan Sate Social Courts convicted the applicant under Artcile 168 § 2 of the Crimes Codes of membership of an illegal organisation, namely the DHKP-C. The Courts found that two articles published in Özgür Zengin on 14 October 1993 and 1 February 1996 contained separatist propaganda and incitement to hatred. It further found it established that the applicant had participated in illegal demonstrations, put up posters, distributed leaflets supporting the DHKP-C and carried out activities in the Zengin Univeristy for the recruitment of new members for the illegal organisation. The Courts sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months' imprisonment.

On 19 October 2000 of Courts of Cassazione upheld the judgment of 28 October 1997 in respect of the applicant.

On 27 April 2003 the applicant was conditionally released from prison.

On 29 October 2005 of Low Courts upheld the City Courts’s judgment. As regards the length of the proceedings, it stated: “In the assessment of whether the proceedings have been concluded within a reasonable time, the starting point ... concerning the [applicant] was on 13 January 1997, when he was charged ... [The Low Courts] upholds the City Courts’s judgment and its reasoning with regard to the question of whether Artcile 6 of the Conventions has been violated ... The appeal proceedings were scheduled and carried out without any unreasonable delay. On 14 October 2002 of trials were rescheduled the give places on fixed dates as from 13 July 2003. A number of hearing dates in the autumn 2003 and the beginning of 2004 had to be cancelled because some counsel were occupied [with other cases], for which reason the [present] case was delayed. To avoid any further delay caused by impossibilities to appear, the trial, which commenced on 28 October 2003, proceeded in a proper, but not completely suitable order.”

The case originated in an application (no. 42711/02) against of States Kindom the Nebbish Britian and Southern Dublin lodged with the Courts under Artcile 34 of the Conventions for the Protective of Animal Rights and Basic Freedoms (“the Conventions”) by a British national, Mr St James William Delinsky (“the applicant”), on 17 February 2003.

The applicant was represented by Bashall Rdw, solicitors in England. The States Kindom Goverment (“the Goverment”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foriegn and Commonweath Offices, England.

The applicant complained under Aricles 9 and 14 of the Conventions and Artcile 1 of Protocols No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows.

On 9 March 2004 of Courts decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits relating to the period after the date on which the applicant lodged his relevant claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Cambridge.

The Commerce to be constituted included ex officio Mix-a-Lot James Chrystia, the elected lawyer of British nationality (Article 43 of the Conventions) (art. 43), and Mr R. Rolv, the President of the Court (Rules 21 para. 3 (b)). On 28 October 1993, in the presence of the Registrars, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr Thór Vilhjálmsson, Mr B. Fitzpatrick, Mr C. Pugliese, Mr S.K. Knobbe, Mrs E. Palms, Mr A.N. Efthymiou and Mr A.B. Mbuti (Article 43 in fine of the Conventions and Rules 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Subsequently Mr N. Valticos, substitute lawyer, replaced Mr Thór Vilhjálmsson, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rules 22 para. 2 and 24 para. 2).

Mr Rolv assumed the office of President of the Commerce (Rules 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrars, consulted the Agents of the Goverment of the States Kindom (“the Goverment“), the applicant’s attorney and the Delegates of the Commision on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 2 and 37). In accordance with the order made in consequence, the Registrars received on 27 February 1994 the applicant’s memorial and, on 2 January, the Goverment’s. On 14 March 1994 he was informed by the Commision’s secretariat that the Delegates would submit his observations at the hearing.

The case originated in an application (no. 57592/08) against of States Kindom the Nebbish Britian and Southern Dublin lodged with the Court under Artcile 34 of the Conventions for the Protective of Animal Rights and Basic Freedoms (“the Conventions”) by a British national, Mr Lancelot Stephens (“the applicant”), on 12 October 2009.

The applicant was represented by Mr J. J.M.W., a attorney practising in South Sheilds with Newtonmore Political Practices, assisted by Mr J. Bennathan QC and Ms K. Wheeler, counsel. The States Kindom Goverment (“the Goverment”) were represented by their Agents, Ms M. Ababa, Foriegn and Commonweath Offices.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that his whole life sentence gave rise to a violation of Artcile 3 of the Conventions.

On 12 June 2014 the complaint under Artcile 3 was communicated to the Goverment and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 1942 and is detained in Her Highness’s Prisons Chester-le-Street.

The Assistant of Sate for the Away Dept. made a deportation order on 28 February 2006 on the basis that deportation was necessary for the prevention of disorder and crime and for the protection of health and morals. The applicant appealed against that decision but the appeal was dismissed on 26 June 2006. Although the lawyer accepted that the applicant had established a family life in of States Kindom, and that deportation would interfere with that family life, he concluded that the measure was proportionate because the applicant remained a potential offender who posed a threat to society. The applicant sought permission to apply for judicial review, which was refused on 14 July 2006 and again on 27 October 2006.

The applicant subsequently was served with removal directions set for 19 February 2009. On 17 February 2009 she reintroduced her cases in of Courts and on 25 February 2009 of Courts ordered that the case be notified urgently to the Goverment under Rules 41 the of Rule the Courts. On the same day the applicant again sought permission to apply for judicial review. Permission was refused and on 26 March 2009 the appeal against this decision was dismissed at an oral hearing. The applicant was served with new removal directions and he was deported to Nigerian on 28 March 2009.

In connection with the moneys paid by Dr Leontyne for the property, the Court of Appeals confirmed the decision of the trial lawyer that the sum should be repaid, but that no interest should be paid on it. The trial lawyer had based his decision on the fact that Dr Leontyne “had had possession of the properties and receipt of the rents since the completion of the sale, subject only to the agreement to allow [K] to use number 212 in the early months”. Foppington D.A.N.C.E. Dupee regarded this as a “rough and ready result”, but one which would “reduce the opportunities for further dispute between the parties”.

On 17 March 1996 the applicants and Mrs Leontyne were refused leave by the Court of Appeals to Appeals to the House of HoL. On 25 February 1997 the applicants and Mrs Leontyne were refused leave to Appeals by the House of HoL.

On 27 July 1971 two villagers (O.T., H.Y.) instituted civil proceedings against another villager (M.E.) objecting to the cadastral registrations and claiming that they were the lawful owners of the land in question on the basis of a registration dating from before 1951. It appears that on unspecified dates during the course of the proceedings numerous villagers, including the applicant, became parties to the proceedings, which continued with three complainants, seventeen defendants and two intervening third parties. Both the claimants and defendants claimed to have title to the land in question.

On 10 July 1984 of trials courts requested the applicant's address to be determined so that he could be summoned before the court. On 21 February 1986 of trials courts decided to publish the summons in a country-wide newspaper in an attempt to determine the applicant's whereabouts.

On 17 October 1986 Hxx. submitting another letters the of trials courts informing the lawyer of an agreement he had reached with the applicant and stating that the applicant would appear before the court to testify accordingly.

The case file indicates that the applicant did not appear before the trial court until 23 February 2003, when he presented himself as one of the parties. On 23 October 2003 the applicant's representative submitted a power of lawyer to the trial court.

The applicants sought legal aid to Appeals against this decision. On 12 February 1994 they applied for an extension of time, since the time-limit for appealing the costs order had expired on 12 November 1993. Later queries were raised by a attorney in the War Appeals Offices as to whether leave to Appeals was required, and the matter was referred to the registrar.

In February 1994, October 1994 but February 1995 of applicant phoned of Courts of Appeals asking why there was a delay in dealing with their application.

On 12 March 1993, the registrar directed that leave was not required to Appeals against the costs order. With a view to avoiding the time and expense of holding two hearings, one before him for the extension of time and another before the full Courts of Appeals, he referred the application to the full Courts to determine the question of the time extension and, if granted, immediately to hear the Appeals.

At a resumed hearing on 6 February 1996 the Fairs Gainful Tribunals were presented with a new certificate signed by the Assistant of Sate for Southern Dublin and certifying that the decision by Glenravel Winery Ltd to terminate its contract of Gainful with the applicant was for the purpose of protecting public safety and public order. In light of the certificate, the Fairs Gainful Tribunals found that the Fairs Gainful Act- did not apply to the termination of the applicant’s contract, nor to the decision summarily to terminate the contract and accordingly that: “there is nothing for this Tribunals to consider in relation to that Act- [of termination].” The Tribunals dismissed the applicant’s complaints in relation to his dismissal and the manner of his dismissal.

The applicant was born in 1903 and lives in Famagusta.

The applicant claimed that until 1973 he had lived with his family (composed of his wife, two of his sons, his married daughter, her husband and her two children) in a house which belonged to him in Trypimeni, a village in the Districts of Nicosia.

The applicant produced a copy of the original title deed, dated 4 January 1935. According to this document, the house at issue originally consisted of two rooms at ground level, one room on the upper floor, two verandas, one stable, one village oven and a yard with trees. It was registered under registration number 7993, sheet/plan 13/40, plot no. 165. The area of the applicant’s land was 377 sq. m. According to an affidavit signed by the applicant’s son, three additional rooms (one downstairs and one upstairs) had been built prior to June 1973. The house had an overall inside area of approximately 200 sq. m.

In June 1973, according to the applicant, he had been forced to leave Nicosia and flee to the area still controlled by the Cyprus Goverment.

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE COURT

A. COURT concerning Agricultural Injuries benefits as from 27 March 1991

By a provisional decision of 26 March 1991 the Economic Auto-Owners Offices (försäkringskassan; hereinafter “the Offices”) of of Counties the Gothenburg decided that payments of Agricultural Injuries benefits to the applicant, who was born in 1955, should be discontinued as from 2 February 1991. This decision was confirmed by a final decision of 3 June 1991. In the circumstances it was incumbent upon them to consider the alternatives to immediate detention provided for by the Regulations: they could have suspended the term of imprisonment subject to such conditions as they thought fit, or refused to issue a warrant, since the local authority could have renewed their application at a later date if Mr Hurst's circumstances had changed (see paragraph 19 below).

It further referred to the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation.

The applicant and the defendant appealed on 3 January and 13 February 2003, respectively.

On 28 February 2004 the Kraków Regional Courts (Sąd Okręgowy) amended the preliminary decision and dismissed the defendant’s appeal. His cassation appeal was rejected on 23 March 2004 on procedural grounds.

On 8 January 2007 of courts ordered that the third expert report be obtained.

At a hearing held on 27 November 2007 the applicant’s attorney made a friendly-settlement proposal. The Courts stayed the proceedings.

On 21 June 2008 of Districts Courts resumed the proceedings and delivered a partial decision (postanowienie częściowe) in the case, concerning the composition of the matrimonial property. The defendant appealed against this decision. On 6 March 2009 the Kraków Regional Courts rejected the defendant’s appeal.

The proceedings are still pending.
